strengths: Extremely extensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple algorithms (FastTD3, FastTD3-SimBaV2, FastSAC, PPO, FQL) and diverse benchmarks (28+ HumanoidBench tasks, IsaacGym, IsaacLab, MTBench, Atari-10/27, and a real-robot Booster T1 transfer task), lending strong external validity to the claims.

The method (SEM) is lightweight, requires no auxiliary losses or additional networks, and the paper explicitly demonstrates it adds negligible wall-clock overhead (Table 2), which is valuable given the compute-efficiency focus of the target baselines.

Solid mechanistic investigation connecting the intervention to underlying causes: a controlled CIFAR-10 toy experiment isolates the effect of non-stationarity on representation collapse, complemented by a formal (if informal) analysis (Theorem 1) linking drift to neuron dormancy.

Good ablation coverage: sweeps over simplex dimensions (V, L), comparisons against alternative structuring methods (Gumbel-softmax+ST, VQ, C-ReLU), and robustness checks across core FastTD3 design choices (batch size, replay buffer size, number of environments, CDQ, C51, noise scale).

Diagnostic metrics (effective rank, dormant neurons, Gini sparsity, Cramér distance, TD error, critic disagreement) are tracked consistently to substantiate why SEM helps, going beyond simple return curves.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Simplicial Embeddings are adopted wholesale from Lavoie et al. (2023) for self-supervised learning and were already used implicitly in TD-MPC2; the contribution is primarily an application/empirical study rather than a new technique.

The formal analysis (Theorem 1) is a loose, first-order/heuristic argument with several approximations (linearization around a moving optimum, bounds using bias terms) rather than a rigorous, tight theoretical guarantee — it supports intuition but shouldn't be over-interpreted as a proof of the central claim.

No direct final-performance comparison against strong sample-efficient baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., TD-MPC2, BRO, SR-SPR) — these are only discussed narratively, leaving open how SEM-augmented fast actor-critic methods compare quantitatively to the sample-efficiency frontier.

Some reported gains appear marginal or within overlapping confidence bands (e.g., several IsaacGym curves in Fig. 17 show near-identical baseline vs. SEM performance), which is not explicitly discussed or quantified with significance tests.

Core mechanistic ablations (Figs. 3-8) are conducted on a reduced 5-task HumanoidBench subset due to compute constraints, and hyperparameters (L, V, τ) are largely fixed at defaults without per-task tuning, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation but which weakens confidence in generality of the specific parameter choices (e.g., V=64).

The writing includes essayistic/promotional framing (e.g., opening philosophical epigraph, narrative connections drawn somewhat post-hoc between correlational diagnostics and performance) that occasionally overstates causal claims from correlational evidence.

strengths: Remarkably broad and thorough empirical evaluation: SEM is tested across FastTD3, FastTD3-SimBaV2, FastSAC, PPO, and Flow-Q-Learning, spanning HumanoidBench (28+ tasks across H1, H1-hand, G1 morphologies), IsaacGym/IsaacLab, MTBench, Atari-10/27 games, OGBench offline-to-online tasks, and even a real/sim-to-real Booster T1 humanoid benchmark.

Mechanistic, multi-angle analysis connecting SEM to representation collapse: effective rank, dormant neuron percentage, feature/weight norms, TD error, critic disagreement (Cramér distance), Gini sparsity, and simplex entropy are all tracked and consistently support the paper's narrative.

Useful and well-motivated ablations: sweeping SEM's L and V hyperparameters, comparing against alternative structuring mechanisms (Gumbel-Softmax+ST, Vector Quantization, C-ReLU), and testing robustness to FastTD3 design choices (CDQ, C51, batch size, replay buffer size, noise scale, number of parallel envs).

The proposed intervention is lightweight (no auxiliary losses, no extra networks), architecturally simple (single softmax-based layer), and reported to add negligible computational overhead, making it easy to adopt in existing fast actor-critic pipelines.

A small supervised (CIFAR-10) toy experiment nicely illustrates the core hypothesis (non-stationarity causes representation collapse; SEM mitigates it) in an interpretable, controlled setting before moving to RL.
Strong reproducibility effort: extensive appendix with hyperparameter tables, architecture descriptions, per-environment learning curves, and metric definitions.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: Simplicial Embeddings were already introduced by Lavoie et al. (2023) and already used by TD-MPC2 (Hansen et al., 2023, explicitly acknowledged in the paper); this work's primary contribution is applying/ablating this existing technique within fast actor-critic pipelines rather than proposing a fundamentally new mechanism.

No comparison against strong dedicated sample-efficient RL baselines (e.g., TD-MPC2, DreamerV3, SR-SPR, BRO) in absolute performance terms; all comparisons are internal (baseline vs. baseline+SEM), so it's unclear how much of the original sample-efficiency gap highlighted in the introduction is actually closed.

The theoretical analysis (Theorem 1/App. B) is informal despite being framed as a 'proof'—it relies on first-order approximations and generic arguments about covariance deflation and gradient gating, but does not derive properties specific to the simplex constraint itself (e.g., why bounding via softmax competition is better than alternative bounding schemes).

The mechanistic diagnostics (effective rank, entropy, sparsity) are largely correlational; the paper shows these metrics move together with performance but does not establish a causal link or rule out confounds (e.g., SEM could simply act as an implicit normalization/regularizer unrelated to its 'simplex' geometry).

The abstract's claim of 'no loss in runtime speed' is only partially supported by Table 2, where several tasks (e.g., h1hand-walk, h1hand-stair) show SEM increasing wall-clock time, and the critic-side runtime cost is not reported.

No statistical significance testing is reported despite the large number of comparisons across tasks/seeds, and hyperparameters (L, V, τ) are fixed globally rather than tuned per task, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation but which limits confidence that reported gains are not partly due to favorable default settings.

The sheer number of figures/ablations, while thorough, sometimes reads as a broad sweep without a single deep, decisive causal experiment isolating exactly which property of SEM (boundedness vs. sparsity vs. group structure) drives the improvement.
